idiom_name: predicate function pointer plus context struct; hand-written and/or/not combinators
implementation_notes: C has neither objects nor closures, so the rule object becomes a struct holding a function pointer and a context pointer, exactly the callback contract the C standard library itself uses (`typedef bool (*spec_fn)(const void *candidate, const void *ctx);` with `struct spec { spec_fn fn; const void *ctx; };`). Combinators are ordinary functions returning a new spec whose context points at an array of child specs - `spec_and(const spec *parts, size_t n)` evaluating children in order with short-circuit, `spec_or`, `spec_not`. The classic structure survives only as this data-plus-function pair; when a rule is used once, pass the function pointer and context straight to a hand-written find/filter loop instead of building combinators.
pitfalls: Context pointers must outlive the specifications that hold them; a combinator whose context points at a caller stack frame dangles as soon as that frame returns, and the standard qsort comparator cannot take context at all, forcing globals or thread-local state.
The candidate arrives as void*, so the rule casts without type checking: a specification applied to the wrong struct is silent memory corruption rather than a compile error.
Combinators need an explicit array plus count and usually malloc/free; a forgotten free leaks, while copying child specifications by value copies stale context pointers.
